An Auditable Public-Data U.S. Equity Research 
Pipeline: 
Point-in-Time Factors, Asset Pricing, Portfolio 
Construction, 
and Walk-Forward Machine Learning 
Amit Kumar Dudi 
Department of Computational Intelligence 
SRM Institute of Science and Technology 
Kattankulathur, Chennai, India 
ak2910@srmist.edu.in 
 
Abstract—This paper studies a public -data U.S. -equity 
research pipeline in which security identity, filing availability, 
source transitions, transaction costs, and temporal validation 
are specified before performance is interpreted. The released 
sample screens 822 securities and admits 487 equities. It 
contains 715,447 daily market observations and 37,273 point-in-
time fundamental observations. Forty -seven of 48 factor 
definitions are estimable. Five asset -pricing families show 
higher mean in -sample adjusted R -squared for multifactor 
specifications (0.259–0.301) than for CAPM (0.063). Eight long-
only portfolio methods are evaluated under ex -ante one -way 
costs of 5, 10, and 20 basis points over a 32 -month factor -
portfolio window. Eight prediction models are assessed i n 17 
purged monthly test folds using two characteristics. Every non-
constant model’s bootstrap interval for mean rank correlation 
includes zero, and stable after -cost incremental value is not 
established. The contribution is a connected empirical design 
that preserves negative and inconclusive findings while making 
the sample’s public-data and short-window limitations explicit. 
Keywords—empirical asset pricing; point-in-time data; factor 
models; portfolio construction; transaction costs; walk -forward 
validation; machine learning; reproducibility 
JEL classifications: C52, C55, G11, G12, G17 
I. INTRODUCTION 
A. Motivation 
Empirical finance often begins after the hardest data 
decisions have already been made. Yet security identity, 
delisting coverage, accounting availability, corporate -action 
treatment, and source changes determine which observations 
a model sees. Portfolio and machine -learning layers add 
further choices about costs, sample splits, tuning, and 
interpretation. This study places those decisions inside one 
versioned workflow and asks what conclusions remain after 
the evidence is bounded explicitly. 
B. Research problem 
The project uses free and public sources rather than CRSP 
or Compustat. That choice expands reproducibility and 
access, but it also creates limitations that cannot be repaired 
by software alone. A fixed upstream ticker universe may omit 
firms that disappeared before the provider snapshot; a change 
from consolidated -tape to IEX -only bars alters volume 
comparability; and SEC facts become usable only after filing 
acceptance. The empirical problem is therefore both statistical 
and evidentiary. 
C. Research questions 
The analysis asks whether factor construction is feasible 
on the selected panel, whether multifactor models improve 
explanatory fit, how long -only allocations differ under fixed
